problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+17y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+17{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16)-16+17 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +4 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-4\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-4\pm \text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(-4+\text{i})x})={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(-4+\text{i})x})={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4{e}^{x}$ is not a solution.
